description: The image displays three pie charts labeled “easy,” “medium,” and “hard,” each representing the distribution of four categories—N+K+, N−K+, N−K−, and N+K−—across different difficulty levels of a task, likely related to knowledge reasoning in large language models as suggested by the paper title. The legend on the right identifies the color coding: teal for N+K+, yellow for N−K+, orange for N−K−, and red for N+K−. In the “easy” chart, N−K+ dominates at 45.9%, followed by N+K+ at 40.6%, N−K− at 10.1%, and N+K− at 3.3%. The “medium” chart shows a more balanced distribution: N+K+ at 44.6%, N−K+ at 44.3%, N−K− at 7.2%, and N+K− at 3.9%. In the “hard” chart, N−K+ and N−K− are nearly equal at 36.2% and 36.8% respectively, with N+K+ at 20.1% and N+K− at 7.0%. All charts include percentage labels inside each slice, and the “CoT” label beneath the middle chart may indicate that these results are conditioned on Chain-of-Thought prompting. The visual layout suggests a comparison of how model performance or behavior shifts across difficulty levels based on whether the model has access to relevant knowledge (K) and whether it generates correct answers (N).
